blocks.text: With these the reader may compare what Gesner, in his Birds, p. 24, reports that he read in the Greek paraphrase of Oppian's Ixeutica: that small birds, in fear of a hawk brought near by the fowler, hide themselves under the foliage of trees and, since they do not dare to fly away, are easily caught. And this passage of Apuleius in the first Apology: "Remember, however, that it would be as ridiculous an argument to say that obscene sea creatures were sought for love affairs as to say that a sea comb was sought for combing hair, or a hawk-fish for catching flying creatures." Finally, nothing is more explicit than these words of Julius Firmicus, who lived under Constantine, in book 5, chapter 7 of the Mathesis, concerning those whose horoscope has Venus in Aquarius: "They will be eager to keep hawks, falcons, goshawks, eagles and birds of this kind, and horses for hunting." And in the following chapter: "If Mercury is found in Virgo, whoever have him so will be strong, industrious, shrewd, breeders of horses, of hawks, of falcons, and of the other birds that belong to fowling." Accordingly, since in the age of Chrysostom, who flourished only at the end of the fourth century, fowling with hawks seems long to have been in wide use, we may well wonder why he placed hawks in the class τῶν ἀχρήστων, καὶ εἰκῆ δοκούντων εἶναι [tōn achrēstōn, kai eikē dokountōn einai]. It could indeed be answered that the great man, being a very strict guardian and rigid attendant of virtue, could have regarded such fowling as superfluous and counted it among the things on which time is uselessly spent. But, as I think more true, most of these passages are little to the point and do not sufficiently establish the antiquity of fowling with hawks. For what is adduced from Ctesias about the Indians, from the Philosopher about the Thracians, and from Pliny about Craterus are rudiments of the art, and these received only among barbarians, not yet among the Greeks. And in Martial and Oppian the hawk deceives or frightens birds, but does not yet catch them. And in Apuleius it is sought for catching birds: not that it may catch them itself, but that it may assist those who catch them. Only Julius Firmicus therefore remains; and since he lived and wrote in an age from which so many records survive, I cannot wonder enough that in that age no one else mentioned so noble a kind of fowling, one notable and memorable for its very novelty. Moreover, the name astures [goshawks], which you read there, occurs nowhere else among the ancients; and therefore these passages are highly suspect to me, and in them the scribes seem to have added something of their own. It is certain, however, that this fowling flourished not long after Chrysostom. For Prosper, who follows immediately after him, says this in On the Contemplative [III, 13] Life, book 3, chapter 17: "They use hawks and fattened dogs for hunting." And Sidonius in the Panegyric to Avitus, his father-in-law, emperor [col. 272] and consul in the year 456:

What of his zeal for birds, which nature makes rapacious against a crowd almost of their own kin? Who more skilfully than he has taught them to join varied combats through the clouds! With a bird he conquers birds, and with swift beating of wings through the air no taloned fighter wages war better for anyone than for him.

And to Herodicus, the son of this Avitus, in Letter 3 of book 3: "Ball, dice-box, hawk, dog, horse, bow were your play." And to Industrius, Letter 9 of book 4, in commendation of the illustrious Vectius: "Those are lighter matters, that he of whom we speak is second to none in training, watching and carrying about horses, dogs and hawks." Thereafter, as luxury grew, since in Gaul the clergy too kept dogs and hawks, many councils throughout the sixth century forbade it: as in the year 506 the Council of Agde, canon 55: "Let it not be lawful for bishops, presbyters and deacons to keep dogs for hunting, or hawks." This same is repeated in the year 517 in canon 4 of the Council of Epaone, and in the year 585 in canon 13 of the second Council of Mâcon: "Where there is the constant singing of God, it is a monstrous thing and a mark of disgrace for dogs or hawks to dwell there." Therefore Leander and Pancirolla, who attribute the invention of this fowling to the emperor Frederick Barbarossa, and Pandolfo Collenuccio, who attributes it to the emperor Henry VI, are gravely mistaken.
